title: De eximio usu methodi interpolationum in serierum doctrina

deep.reconstruction:
Context (E555, §§40–44). Euler's interpolation method makes a curve pass through prescribed ordinates at the abscissae nθ, (1−n)θ, (1+n)θ, (2−n)θ, … . Here the ordinates are +f, +f, −f, −f, +f, … . In §43 he takes θ = π and f = sin nπ, so every data point lies on the sine curve y = sin x. His interpolation formula gives a closed-form relation for the ordinate y at abscissa x = ωπ:

  nΔy / ((n−ω) sin nπ) = π cos nπ · sin ωπ / ( sin(n−ω)π · sin(n+ω)π ).

The factor Δ = Δ(n, ω) comes out of his method as a quotient of Eulerian (Beta) integrals.

The question. Infinitely many curves pass through the same points, so it is not automatic that the interpolant equals sin ωπ off the nodes. It is known to hold for ω = 0, ω = ±(1±n), and for infinitesimal ω. At ω = 0,

  Δ = ∫z^{n−1}(1−z)^{−n} dz · ∫z^{n−1}(1−z)^{n} dz / ∫z^{n−1}(1−z)^{−2n} dz = π cot nπ.

In modern terms this is B(n,1−n)·B(n,n+1)/B(n,1−2n). The reflection and duplication-type identities give exactly π cos nπ / sin nπ.

Rewriting Δ. Euler uses

  ∫z^{n+ω−1}(1−z)^{−n−ω} / ∫z^{n+ω−1}(1−z)^{−2n} = (1−2n) ∫z^{ω−n}(1−z)^{−n−ω} (for n < 1/2).

In Gamma form both sides equal Γ(1+ω−n)Γ(1−n−ω)/Γ(1−2n). Hence

  Δ = (1−2n) B(1+ω−n, 1−n−ω) · B(n+ω, 1+n−ω).

If y = sin ωπ identically, one would need

  Δ = (n−ω)π sin nπ cos nπ / ( n sin(n−ω)π sin(n+ω)π ).

So the question reduces to a Beta-integral identity.

Numerical test (p.197). Take n = 1/4, ω = 1/2.
- Right side: (−π/8) / ((1/4)(−1/2)) = π.
- Left side: (1/2)∫z^{1/4}(1−z)^{−3/4} · ∫z^{−1/4}(1−z)^{−1/4}.
- Substituting z = v^4 gives 8∫v^4 dv/(1−v^4)^{3/4} · ∫v^2 dv/(1−v^4)^{1/4}.
- Euler's reduction ∫v^{p+λ−1}(1−v^λ)^{q/λ−1} = p/(p+q)·∫v^{p−1}(1−v^λ)^{q/λ−1} turns this into 4∫dv/(1−v^4)^{3/4} · ∫v^2 dv/(1−v^4)^{1/4}.
- This equals (1/4)·B(1/4,1/4)·B(3/4,3/4) = π. Confirmed.

Theorem §44. For all n, ω,

  (1−2n) ∫₀¹ z^{ω−n}(1−z)^{−n−ω} dz · ∫₀¹ z^{n+ω−1}(1−z)^{n−ω} dz = (n−ω)π sin nπ cos nπ / ( n sin(n−ω)π sin(n+ω)π ).

The proof on p.198–199 sets n+ω = μ/λ, ω−n = ν/λ. It then uses his (p/q) calculus of integrals ∫v^{p−1}(1−v^λ)^{q/λ−1} dv: the recursion, the reflection (λ−p / p) = π/(λ sin pπ/λ), and the symmetry (p/q)(p+q/r) = (p/r)(p+r/q).

Modern check. The left side is Γ(1+ω−n)Γ(1−n−ω)Γ(n+ω)Γ(1+n−ω) / (Γ(1−2n)Γ(1+2n)). Applying the reflection formula three times gives π(n−ω)π / (sin(n+ω)π sin(n−ω)π) · sin 2nπ/(2nπ), which is the right side. The theorem is correct, and so the interpolant reproduces sin ωπ for every ω.
errors: No mathematical errors found on this page; the Beta-ratio identity, the n=1/4, ω=1/2 test (both sides = π), and the theorem all check via Gamma reflection.

The normalization of the curve equation here (factor n/((n−ω) sin nπ) on the left, π cos nπ sin ωπ on the right) differs from the transcription of p.194 (π/(f(n−ω)) and 2π cos nπ sin ωπ). Since f = sin nπ, this is most likely a transcription garble on the previous page rather than Euler's error. The condition n<1/2 for the integral rewrite is needed (convergence of ∫(1−z)^{−2n}), as Euler states.

ideas.what: Recognition that agreement of an interpolating curve at infinitely many nodes does not by itself identify it with the 'natural' function (sine); explicit verification needed off the nodes
ideas.modern_name: uniqueness problem for interpolation of entire functions (cf. Carlson-type theorems, cardinal interpolation)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Carlson (1914), Whittaker (1915) for rigorous uniqueness/cardinal series; the caution itself is folklore
ideas.where_published: E555 itself (Nova Acta 1783); similar caveats in Euler's interpolation papers on the Gamma function

ideas.what: Identity (1−2n)B(1+ω−n,1−n−ω)B(n+ω,1+n−ω) = (n−ω)π sin nπ cos nπ/(n sin(n−ω)π sin(n+ω)π)
ideas.modern_name: consequence of Euler's reflection formula Γ(x)Γ(1−x)=π/sin πx applied to Beta products
ideas.where_published: Euler's papers on integrals ∫x^{p−1}(1−x^n)^{q/n−1} (e.g. E321 and related 'Observationes circa integralia formularum'), using his (p/q) notation

ideas.what: Numerical/special-case check via z=v^4 reducing to lemniscate-type integrals ∫dv/(1−v^4)^{3/4}·∫v²dv/(1−v^4)^{1/4}=π/4
ideas.where_published: Euler's papers on integrals of the form ∫x^{p-1}(1-x^n)^{q/n-1}dx (exact E-numbers unsure)

missed.claim: The page treats interpolation through two interleaved shifted lattices (n+ℤ and −n+ℤ) with infinite-product weights. It explicitly raises whether such an interpolant coincides with sin off the nodes, and settles it for this case by a Gamma identity. This is an early instance of the cardinal/sampling-interpolation uniqueness question, which is not usually cited in histories of the Whittaker–Shannon/Carlson line. The mathematics itself is routine.
missed.quote: Hinc autem non sequitur ipsam curuam, quam aequatio inuenta exhibet, esse lineam sinuum, cum innumerabiles aliae curuae per eadem puncta data transire queant.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical: an 18th-century awareness of non-uniqueness in infinite interpolation, a theme later formalized in entire function theory. Of minor interest only.

deep.surprise_reason: The theorem is a correct but routine consequence of Beta/Gamma reflection, proved with Euler's known (p/q) calculus. The only notable point is the explicit methodological caution about non-uniqueness of the interpolating curve, which is modestly interesting historically.
transcription_corrections: Curve equation: right side numerator should read 'π cos.nπ · sin.ωπ' (image: πcof.nπ.fin.ωπ), not 'πω f.nπ.sin.ωπ'.
'ita vt sit Δ = πω/sin.nπ' should read 'Δ = π cos.nπ / sin.nπ' (consistent with the Beta-integral expression at ω=0).
